answer.rationale: The binding constraints are the 18% cost mandate and a line running at 94% of committed volume with no buffer, with the contract lapsing in 14 days. That combination rules out several directions immediately: negotiate_terms (memory_c4, memory_c6) presupposes a counterparty willing to reopen price, and the incumbent has already refused this cycle, so the mechanism those memories describe is not available; defer_decision (memory_c5) worked on a non-critical, auto-continuing service, whereas this contract does not auto-renew and lapsing it on a zero-buffer line converts a cost problem into a stoppage; renew_incumbent (memory_c1) protects continuity but concedes the mandate entirely. That leaves a full switch or a second source. memory_c2 is the single most load-bearing memory for the switch case, so it is the one worth spending the verification pull on. Its wording is also where I am most suspicious: it credits unit cost, onboarding speed, and invoicing accuracy, but says nothing about on-time delivery, quality yield, or whether the volume moved was comparable to a line at committed capacity. Invoicing accuracy is an accounts-payable virtue being cited in a delivery-risk decision, which is exactly the kind of substitution that survives consolidation because it sounds like diligence. I want the archived record to tell me the component, the share of volume moved, and whether any delivery or defect data was captured; if the original only ever measured price and paperwork, memory_c2 cannot carry a full primary-supply move against a 94% line. add_second_source (memory_c3) is the action that does not require resolving that uncertainty first: it qualifies the alternate vendor on a small guarded share, starts recovering cost against the mandate, restores the negotiating leverage the incumbent's refusal removed, and keeps the incumbent flowing so the line is never dependent on an unproven counterparty. Scale is deliberately a small guarded test rather than a broad rollout, because at 94% utilization a bad allocation has no slack to absorb it. Residual risks I am not resolving this cycle: a partial second source likely will not reach 18% on its own, so the gap carries to the next review; qualification effort on a 14-day clock is real; and memory_c3's shortage-era success was about allocation security, not cost, so I should not assume it transfers to the savings case. If verification shows memory_c2 did track delivery performance at comparable volume, switch_primary_vendor becomes the stronger candidate at the next review.
